ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study protocol was reviewed and approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of the author's institution.
Participants were informed that they would interact with an AI chatbot and that the messages displayed during the interaction were AI-generated.
Participants were recruited from Prolific, an online crowdsourcing platform designed for research purposes, from April 16 -17, 2026.
Eligible participants were Prolific users who were 21 years or older, current e-cigarette users, living in the United States, and had a previous approval rate of at least 98%.
The primary structural equation modeling (SEM) analyses included participants assigned to the two chatbot conditions.
Approximately 185 additional participants were targeted for the staticmessage condition, producing a total target of at least 555 qualified participants.
A total of 692 participants were recruited. 89 did not meet the eligibility criteria, and 17 failed at least one of two attention checks.
Participants had a mean age of 38.56 years (SD = 11.51); 44.4% identified as male and 54.8% as female.
All participants provided informed consent electronically before participating in the study.

Vaping status was categorized according to the number of days participants had used ecigarettes during the previous 30 days: infrequent use (1-5 days), intermediate use (6-27 days), or daily use (28-30 days; Amato et al., 2016).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. keywords: Xingman Wu: Conceptualization, Methodology, Software, Investigation, Data curation, Formal analysis, Visualization, Writing -original draft, Writing -review & editing AI chatbot

text.text: AI chatbots are increasingly used to deliver health information and persuasive interventions, yet the consequences of making these systems appear humanlike remain unclear.

Drawing on the Computers Are Social Actors and Media Are Social Actors paradigms, mind perception theory, and psychological reactance theory, this research examined whether anthropomorphism in AI chatbots shapes reactance through two competing pathways: trust in the chatbot and perceived persuasive intent.
An online between-subjects experiment was conducted among U.S. adults who currently used e-cigarettes.
Participants in the main study (N = 586) were randomly assigned to interact with either an anthropomorphic or a non-anthropomorphic AI chatbot, or to view a static vaping cessation message.

The results showed that interacting with an anthropomorphized chatbot reduced reactance compared to reading a static message, although this advantage did not extend to attitudes toward vaping or intentions to quit.
Additionally, while anthropomorphism can generally reduce psychological reactance, its two dimensions, mindful and mindless anthropomorphism, operated in different paths.
Mindful anthropomorphism was associated with greater trust and, indirectly, lower reactance.
Mindless anthropomorphism was directly associated with lower reactance.
These findings support the potential use of anthropomorphic AI chatbots as a communication approach for vaping cessation.

Furthermore, by distinguishing mindful from mindless anthropomorphism and clarifying their distinct mechanisms, this research offers a more nuanced explanation of how humanlike AI cues shape psychological reactance and provides practical guidance for designing AI-mediated health interventions.
AI chatbots have become widely used in customer service, e-commerce, education, and health care (Adam et al., 2021; Adamopoulou & Moussiades, 2020; Labadze et al., 2023; Laymouna et al., 2024).

text.text: As chatbots take on more service and support roles traditionally performed by people, designers often equip them with humanlike social cues to make interactions feel more natural and engaging.
These cues can take verbal, visual, auditory, or behavioral forms, including human names, facial expressions, small talk, and first turn (Feine et al., 2019).
text.formatted: These cues can take verbal, visual, auditory, or behavioral forms, including human names, facial expressions, small talk, and first turn <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Feine et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: As AI chatbots increasingly evolve beyond providing information to advising and encouraging users, an important question arises: whether making these agents more humanlike can improve their effectiveness as persuasive communicators.
The growing use of humanlike design seems to be grounded in the assumption that anthropomorphism will improve users' experience and responses to AI chatbots.

Indeed, some existing research has found that chatbot anthropomorphism can elicit greater social presence, trust, satisfaction, acceptance, and compliance (Adam et al., 2021; Cheng et al., 2023; Ischen et al., 2020; Song et al., 2024; Zhang & Sheng, 2026).

text.text: However, in persuasive communication, anthropomorphism may produce backfire effects.
On one hand, a humanlike chatbot may appear more competent and benevolent, thereby increasing trust and reducing reactance to its recommendations (Murtaza et al., 2024; Park et al., 2023).

text.text: On the other hand, humanlike qualities may lead users to perceive the chatbot as possessing greater agency and acting with intentions to influence (Gray et al., 2007; Waytz et al., 2010).

text.text: This heightened perception of perceived persuasive intent could, in turn, increase users' psychological reactance and weaken their attitudes toward and intentions to follow the recommendations (Reynolds-Tylus, 2019).

text.text: Anthropomorphism may therefore facilitate or undermine persuasion depending on the strength of these two competing pathways.

The proposed negative pathway is centered around psychological reactance, referring to "the motivational state that is hypothesized to occur when a freedom is eliminated or threatened with elimination" (Brehm & Brehm, 1981, p. 37).

text.text: These consequences are particularly concerning in health communication, where reactance to recommendations such as quitting vaping, reducing alcohol consumption, or getting vaccinated can directly undermine individuals' health outcomes.

Understanding which pathway between anthropomorphism and reactance predominates is therefore vital for designing AI chatbots that effectively promote health behavior change while minimizing reactance.
Before exploring the relationship between anthropomorphism and psychological reactance, it is necessary to first understand anthropomorphism.
Broadly speaking, anthropomorphism refers to the attribution of humanlike characteristics, motivations, intentions, or emotions to nonhuman entities (Epley et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Broadly speaking, anthropomorphism refers to the attribution of humanlike characteristics, motivations, intentions, or emotions to nonhuman entities <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Epley et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Although most existing studies treated anthropomorphism as a single construct, some scholars have distinguished between mindful and mindless modes of anthropomorphism (Kim & Sundar, 2012).
text.formatted: Although most existing studies treated anthropomorphism as a single construct, some scholars have distinguished between mindful and mindless modes of anthropomorphism <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Kim & Sundar, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Mindful anthropomorphism involves deliberate attribution, whereas mindless anthropomorphism occurs more automatically (Kim & Sundar, 2012; Lombard & Xu, 2021).
text.formatted: Mindful anthropomorphism involves deliberate attribution, whereas mindless anthropomorphism occurs more automatically <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Kim & Sundar, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Lombard & Xu, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Existing studies have yielded mixed evidence regarding whether chatbot anthropomorphic cues elicit both modes in the same or opposite direction (Araujo, 2018; Kim & Sundar, 2012; Li et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Existing studies have yielded mixed evidence regarding whether chatbot anthropomorphic cues elicit both modes in the same or opposite direction <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Araujo, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Kim & Sundar, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Li et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: This indicates that mindful and mindless anthropomorphism may capture distinct aspects of the construct, and both should be measured in the study.

Therefore, the present study examines the relationship between anthropomorphism and psychological reactance through two models: one treating anthropomorphism as a single general construct, and the other distinguishing mindful and mindless anthropomorphism as two correlated individual constructs.
Estimating and comparing the two models provides a more comprehensive understanding of the mechanisms through which anthropomorphism shapes psychological reactance and its downstream outcomes.

With the development of Large Language Models (LLMs), AI chatbots have emerged as a promising approach to smoking/vaping cessation due to their accessibility and capacity to deliver personalized, real-time conversations (Liu et al., 2025).
text.formatted: With the development of Large Language Models (LLMs), AI chatbots have emerged as a promising approach to smoking/vaping cessation due to their accessibility and capacity to deliver personalized, real-time conversations <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Liu et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, limited research has investigated the effectiveness of AI chatbot-mediated interventions for vaping cessation.
Moreover, vaping cessation is a particularly relevant context in which to examine psychological reactance.
Unlike commercial chatbot interactions, vaping cessation conversations aim to change users' existing behaviors, which can directly threaten their perceived freedom.
This makes reactance more likely to occur, providing an appropriate context in which to test whether and how anthropomorphism shapes reactance and its outcomes.
Given that AI chatbot-mediated persuasion is a relatively new area of research, important questions remain unanswered about how anthropomorphism shapes persuasive outcomes.

In particular, little research has examined the competing pathways through which anthropomorphism may influence psychological reactance and its downstream outcomes, and even less has distinguished how mindful and mindless anthropomorphism may function differently in this process.
Therefore, to address the research gap, this study investigated two broad questions: First, does interacting with an AI chatbot produce different outcomes than viewing a static message?

Second, does anthropomorphism shape users' psychological reactance after interacting with an AI chatbot (anthropomorphic vs. non-anthropomorphic) about vaping cessation, and if so, do perceived persuasive intent and trust in the chatbot explain this relationship?
To answer these two questions, adult e-cigarette users were assigned to interact with either an anthropomorphic or non-anthropomorphic AI chatbot or to read a static cessation message.

The study estimated two structural models, one treating anthropomorphism as a single construct and the other distinguishing mindful and mindless anthropomorphism as two correlated constructs, and examined perceived persuasive intent and trust in the AI chatbot as competing pathways to psychological reactance, with attitudes toward vaping and intentions to quit as downstream outcomes.

text.text: AI chatbots have been used to promote physical activity, healthy eating, weight management, medication adherence, vaccination, mental health, and tobacco cessation (Aggarwal et al., 2023; Chan et al., 2024; Oh et al., 2021).

text.text: Several characteristics make chatbots suitable for health persuasion.

They can use real-time user input to tailor information and feedback, remain available outside clinical hours, and allow people to discuss sensitive issues with lower fear of social judgment than they might experience with another person (Aggarwal et al., 2023; Carrasco-Hernandez et al., 2020; Maher et al., 2020).

text.text: Conversational language and responsive turn-taking may also provide a sense of emotional support.

The Computers Are Social Actors (CASA) paradigm explains why people may respond socially to interactive technologies.

CASA argues that people often apply interpersonal scripts and social norms automatically when computers display recognizable social cues, even when they know they are interacting with a machine (Nass & Moon, 2000; Nass et al., 1994).
text.formatted: CASA argues that people often apply interpersonal scripts and social norms automatically when computers display recognizable social cues, even when they know they are interacting with a machine <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Nass & Moon, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Nass et al., 1994)</ref>.

text.text: Two conditions are especially important.

The technology must present enough cues to invite a social response, and users must perceive the technology as an autonomous source of communication rather than only a channel carrying another person's message (Gambino et al., 2020; Nass & Steuer, 1993).
text.formatted: The technology must present enough cues to invite a social response, and users must perceive the technology as an autonomous source of communication rather than only a channel carrying another person's message <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Gambino et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Nass & Steuer, 1993)</ref>.

text.text: Contemporary AI chatbots are capable of eliciting social responses because they satisfy both criteria.
First, AI chatbots can present sufficient social cues, as they communicate through natural language in a conversational, turn-taking manner.
Second, AI chatbots can be perceived as autonomous message sources by design, as they generate their own responses in real time rather than transmitting messages authored by humans.
These features lead users to respond to AI chatbots socially, even when they consciously recognize that they are interacting with an artificial system (Nass & Moon, 2000).
text.formatted: These features lead users to respond to AI chatbots socially, even when they consciously recognize that they are interacting with an artificial system <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Nass & Moon, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: CASA was initially explained through mindlessness: people automatically apply familiar interpersonal scripts when technologies display social cues.
Early CASA scholars generally distinguished this process from anthropomorphism, which was often understood as a conscious attribution of human qualities to nonhuman entities.

However, drawing on Sundar's (2004) earlier observation that anthropomorphism could result from users' long-term social associations with computers, Kim and Sundar (2012) directly challenged this distinction, arguing that anthropomorphism does not need to be conscious.
text.formatted: However, drawing on <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">Sundar's (2004)</ref> earlier observation that anthropomorphism could result from users' long-term social associations with computers, <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Kim and Sundar (2012)</ref> directly challenged this distinction, arguing that anthropomorphism does not need to be conscious.

text.text: In a 2×2 experiment, they manipulated the presence of a human-like agent and the level of interactivity to examine whether these cues would produce mindful and mindless anthropomorphism.

Mindful anthropomorphism was measured by asking participants whether the website seemed humanlike, natural, or lifelike, whereas mindless anthropomorphism was measured using four items that asked whether the website appeared likeable, sociable, friendly, and personal.

The results showed that participants exposed to the humanlike agent reported lower mindful anthropomorphism but higher mindless anthropomorphism compared to those who were not exposed to the humanlike agent.

Additionally, participants in the high-interactivity condition reported higher mindless anthropomorphism but the same level of mindful anthropomorphism compared to those in the low-interactivity condition.
The results revealed that mindful and mindless anthropomorphism are empirically distinguishable.
Users who explicitly deny that an agent is humanlike can still perceive it in a social way (Kim & Sundar, 2012).
text.formatted: Users who explicitly deny that an agent is humanlike can still perceive it in a social way <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Kim & Sundar, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Based on these findings, Lombard and Xu (2021) extended the CASA paradigm by proposing that mindlessness and anthropomorphism are not competing explanations but complementary mechanisms within the MASA paradigm.

text.text: When social cues are high in quality and quantity, users may respond automatically, reflecting mindless anthropomorphism; when social cues are weaker or less sufficient, users may respond deliberately, reflecting mindful anthropomorphism (Kim & Sundar, 2012; Lombard & Xu, 2021).

text.text: Building on the theoretical origins above, mindful and mindless anthropomorphism represent two distinct modes through which users perceive media agents as humanlike.

Mindful anthropomorphism refers to the deliberate and thoughtful attribution of human traits and characteristics to the media agent, whereas mindless anthropomorphism refers to the nonconscious, intuitive, and spontaneous attribution of such traits and characteristics (Nass & Moon, 2000; Kim & Sundar, 2012; Lombard & Xu, 2021).

text.text: Empirical findings support the distinction but do not show one fixed relationship between the dimensions. Kim and Sundar (2012) found that humanlike and interactive cues affected mindful and mindless anthropomorphism differently. Araujo (2018), by contrast, found that anthropomorphic cues in a text-based customer-service chatbot increased both dimensions.

text.text: These findings justify examining a general anthropomorphism construct while also estimating mindful and mindless anthropomorphism separately.

The three-factor theory of anthropomorphism posits that anthropomorphism operates as an inductive inference process through which people apply knowledge about humans to nonhuman targets (Epley et al., 2007).

text.text: Through this process, people may attribute humanlike characteristics, motivations, intentions, and emotions to the imagined or actual behavior of nonhuman agents (Epley et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Through this process, people may attribute humanlike characteristics, motivations, intentions, and emotions to the imagined or actual behavior of nonhuman agents <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Epley et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Mind perception theory further organizes these attributed capacities into two categories: experience and agency (Gray et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Mind perception theory further organizes these attributed capacities into two categories: experience and agency <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Gray et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Experience refers to the capacity to sense and feel, encompassing capacities such as hunger, fear, pain, and pleasure.

Agency, in contrast, refers to the capacity to think, plan, and act intentionally, encompassing capacities such as self-control, morality, planning, and thought (Gray et al., 2007; Waytz et al., 2010).

text.text: Perceived agency of chatbots deserves attention in the context of persuasion because it may shape how users interpret the chatbot's intentions.

When users attribute agency to a chatbot, they may be more likely to interpret its recommendations or messages as deliberate attempts to influence their attitudes or behaviors, resulting in greater perceived persuasive intent.
Heightened perceived persuasive intent may subsequently increase psychological reactance, potentially weakening the persuasiveness of the messages.

Perceived persuasive intent refers to "a target's perception of an agent's strategic behavior in presenting information designed to influence someone's beliefs, attitudes, decisions, or actions" (Friestad & Wright, 1994).
text.formatted: Perceived persuasive intent refers to "a target's perception of an agent's strategic behavior in presenting information designed to influence someone's beliefs, attitudes, decisions, or actions" <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Friestad & Wright, 1994)</ref>.

text.text: Empirical evidence suggests that higher perceived persuasive intent can heighten psychological reactance (Moyer-Guse & Nabi, 2010; Reynolds-Tylus, 2019; van Noort et al., 2012).

Anthropomorphism is positively associated with perceived persuasive intent.
Perceived persuasive intent is positively associated with psychological reactance.

Trust is particularly relevant when people receive health information from an AI chatbot.

The processes that generate a model's response are difficult for most users to inspect, and users must decide whether the system is capable of providing reliable assistance and whether it is oriented toward their interests.

Trust in automation can therefore be understood as willingness to accept vulnerability based on positive expectations that an agent can help achieve a goal under uncertainty (Lee & See, 2004; Rousseau et al., 1998).

text.text: In turn, greater trust may reduce psychological reactance.

When users perceive a chatbot as capable of providing reliable services and as oriented toward their interests, they may be less likely to view its recommendations as threatening to their freedom and experience less reactance (Brendel et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2021).

Anthropomorphism is positively associated with trust in the AI chatbot.
Trust in the AI chatbot is negatively associated with psychological reactance.

Proposed by Brehm in 1966, psychological reactance theory (PRT) suggests that individuals believe they have certain behavioral freedoms.
When these freedoms are threatened or eliminated, the motive to reassert them will be aroused (Brehm, 1966).

text.text: This restoration can occur directly or indirectly (Dillard & Shen, 2005): Direct restoration of the freedom involves adopting a position or behavior opposite from the position or behavior advocated (Worchel & Brehm, 1971).

Method 3.1 Study context This study investigated the proposed hypotheses in the context of vaping-cessation messages delivered by AI chatbots.
Vaping cessation was selected for two reasons.
First, ecigarette use remains a substantial public health concern in the United States.
In 2024, approximately 7.0% of U.S. adults reported current e-cigarette use (National Center for Health Statistics [NCHS], 2025).

Vaping has been associated with cardiovascular, respiratory, neurological, and oral-health risks (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention [CDC], 2025; Nagy et al., 2025; Seiler-Ramadas et al., 2020), underscoring the continued need for effective cessation communication.
Second, vaping cessation provides a theoretically relevant setting for examining psychological reactance.

Although communication campaigns and interventions have sought to discourage e-cigarette use (Ma et al., 2023; Mylocopos et al., 2024; Reiter et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024), strongly worded recommendations may threaten users' perceived freedom and produce resistance.

text.text: For example, ever-vapers exposed to dogmatic public service announcements reported greater perceived freedom threat and psychological reactance than those exposed to suggestive messages (Clayton et al., 2020; Clayton et al., 2023).
text.formatted: For example, ever-vapers exposed to dogmatic public service announcements reported greater perceived freedom threat and psychological reactance than those exposed to suggestive messages <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Clayton et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Clayton et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Vaping cessation is therefore a suitable context for investigating whether the design of a persuasive technology can reduce resistance to health recommendations.
AI chatbots were chosen as the communication format because emerging evidence suggests that conversational agents may support tobacco-cessation efforts.
Engagement with Aipaca, a GPT-4-powered cessation chatbot, was associated with improvements in health-risk knowledge, cessation knowledge, self-efficacy, and readiness to quit (Liu et al., 2025).

text.text: Similarly, a pilot randomized controlled trial found higher three-month smoking-abstinence rates among QuitBot users than among users of the National Cancer Institute's SmokefreeTXT program (Bricker et al., 2024).

text.text: These findings suggest that AI chatbots may offer a promising channel for delivering cessation information and support.
To create a real-time conversational experience, the GPT-4.1-mini API was embedded in the online survey.
Participants were informed that they would interact with an AI chatbot and that the messages displayed during the interaction were AI-generated.
Participants in both chatbot conditions completed three conversational rounds.
Anthropomorphism was manipulated through the chatbot's system instructions, which were developed using the COSTAR prompting framework (Teo, 2025).
text.formatted: Anthropomorphism was manipulated through the chatbot's system instructions, which were developed using the COSTAR prompting framework <ref type="bibr">(Teo, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The manipulation varied the chatbot's assigned role, communication style, and tone.

In the anthropomorphic condition, the chatbot was instructed to act as a warm, friendly, and personally engaged conversational partner, communicate naturally, demonstrate attentiveness, and refer to information previously shared by the participant.

In the non-anthropomorphic condition, it was instructed to act as a neutral informational tool and communicate in a clear, impersonal, task-focused, and robot-like manner without conveying warmth, personality, or social presence.
All other major instructions were held constant across the two chatbot conditions.
Both chatbots were instructed to provide accurate information about vaping risks and cessation strategies, tailor their responses to participants' input, and help participants consider quitting.
Responses were limited to 120-150 words and were required to remain consistent with guidance from the NIH, CDC, or FDA.
The chatbots were also instructed not to diagnose participants or provide medical advice and to refer users to qualified professionals when appropriate.
The complete system prompts are provided in the Appendix A.
Before the interaction, participants answered an open-ended question about their experiences with vaping and thoughts about quitting.
Their response was provided to the chatbot to support personalized communication.
Conversation history was retained and transmitted to the model during each round, allowing subsequent responses to incorporate participants' earlier statements.

Although the exact wording and information generated by the chatbot varied across participants, the two conditions shared the same persuasive objective, authoritative information sources, response-length requirements, safety constraints, number of conversational rounds, and access to participants' previous input (specific prompts can be found in Appendix A).
Participants in the static-message condition read a fixed 127-word vaping-cessation message.

The message was developed based on content patterns identified during repeated developmental interactions with both chatbot versions and addressed three topics commonly covered across the chatbot conversations: the health risks of vaping, the benefits of quitting, and possible cessation strategies.
Consistent with the chatbot instructions, the message presented information derived from authoritative health sources.
The complete static message is provided in Appendix A.
The static condition served as a noninteractive benchmark rather than a fully dosagematched control.
Unlike participants in the chatbot conditions, participants in this condition did not receive personalized responses or engage in multiple conversational rounds.

Therefore, comparisons between either chatbot condition and the static-message condition capture the broader effects of chatbot-based communication, including interactivity, personalization, and additional message exposure.
However, the comparison between the anthropomorphic and nonanthropomorphic chatbot conditions provides a more controlled test of the anthropomorphism manipulation.

text.text: An online experiment was conducted using a between-subjects design with three conditions: a non-anthropomorphized AI chatbot condition, an anthropomorphized AI chatbot condition, and a static message control condition.
Participants were recruited from Prolific, an online crowdsourcing platform designed for research purposes, from April 16 -17, 2026.
Eligible participants were Prolific users who were 21 years or older, current e-cigarette users, living in the United States, and had a previous approval rate of at least 98%.
Current e-cigarette users were defined as individuals who used e-cigarettes in the past 30 days and had not already quit (Cuccia et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Current e-cigarette users were defined as individuals who used e-cigarettes in the past 30 days and had not already quit <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Cuccia et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Qualified participants who agreed to participate were offered $2.20 for completing the 15-minute study.
After screening and providing informed consent, eligible participants reported their vaping status and perceptions of vaping.
They were then randomly assigned to one of the three conditions.

Participants in the chatbot conditions completed three rounds of interaction about vaping with a pre-prompted chatbot powered by the GPT-4.1-mini API (Costello et al., 2024), whereas those in the control condition read a static persuasive message discouraging vaping.

text.text: Following exposure, chatbot participants reported perceived anthropomorphism, response coherence, perceived intelligence, trust, perceived persuasive intent, psychological reactance, attitudes toward vaping, and intentions to quit.
They also reported general trust in and familiarity with AI chatbots; these covariates were measured after exposure to minimize priming.

text.text: Mindful anthropomorphism was assessed with three 7point semantic differential items (e.g., machinelike -humanlike; Cronbach's α = .943).

Perceived persuasive intent was measured by three items adapted from van Noort et al.

As a motivational state, latent variable psychological reactance cannot be measured directly.

This study examined whether and how AI chatbot anthropomorphism shapes psychological reactance to vaping-cessation messages.

Participants assigned to the anthropomorphic chatbot condition reported less reactance than those who read the static message, whereas the non-anthropomorphic chatbot did not differ significantly from the static message.
The SEM results further clarified the mechanisms underlying these responses.
General anthropomorphism was associated with greater trust in the chatbot, which was subsequently associated with lower reactance.
By contrast, anthropomorphism was not associated with perceived persuasive intent, although perceived persuasive intent was associated with greater reactance.

Moreover, mindful and mindless anthropomorphism followed distinct pathways: mindful anthropomorphism was indirectly associated with lower reactance through trust, whereas mindless anthropomorphism was directly associated with lower reactance.
These findings demonstrate that anthropomorphism is not a unitary process and that its dimensions may facilitate receptivity to persuasive AI communication in different ways.
This study extends research on chatbot anthropomorphism to health persuasion.
Unlike many commercial interactions, vaping-cessation communication explicitly encourages users to change an established behavior and may therefore threaten perceived freedom.

The finding that an anthropomorphic chatbot elicited less reactance than a static message suggests that conversational and humanlike communication may help reduce resistance to health recommendations, even when the advocated behavioral change is potentially freedom threatening.
The findings also distinguish two mechanisms through which anthropomorphism could influence reactance.
General anthropomorphism was associated with greater trust, which, in turn, was associated with lower reactance.
Users who perceived the chatbot as more humanlike may have regarded it as more credible, dependable, or responsive to their needs and consequently experienced its recommendations as less threatening.
Trust therefore appears to be an important mechanism connecting perceived anthropomorphism with receptivity to health messages.
In contrast, anthropomorphism was not associated with perceived persuasive intent.

This null finding is theoretically informative because it suggests that perceiving humanlike qualities in an AI chatbot does not necessarily lead users to infer that the system is attempting to influence them.
A central contribution of this study is its distinction between mindful and mindless anthropomorphism.
The measurement and structural models separating the two dimensions fit the data better than the models treating all seven items as a single anthropomorphism construct.
More importantly, the dimensions exhibited different relationships with trust and reactance.
Mindful anthropomorphism was associated with lower reactance primarily through greater trust, whereas mindless anthropomorphism was instead directly associated with lower reactance.
These patterns extend the CASA/MASA perspective by showing that conscious perceptions of humanlikeness and automatic social responses are not interchangeable.
Treating anthropomorphism as a single construct could conceal the different processes through which humanlike AI communication shapes persuasion.
Future theory and measurement should therefore specify which form of anthropomorphism is expected to operate and why.
The findings offer several implications for the design of health-focused AI chatbots.
Designers may be able to reduce reactance by developing chatbots that communicate in a socially responsive and personable manner while cultivating users' trust.
In particular, the distinct role of mindful anthropomorphism suggests that humanlike communication may reduce reactance when it strengthens trust.
The direct association between mindless anthropomorphism and lower reactance further highlights the potential value of making chatbots appear or sound likeable, friendly, sociable, and personal.

The absence of an association between anthropomorphism and perceived persuasive intent is also encouraging, although it should not be interpreted as evidence that anthropomorphic design is universally risk free.
In the present context, increasing anthropomorphism did not appear to make the chatbot's persuasive purpose more salient.
Designers may therefore be able to incorporate humanlike conversational features without necessarily increasing users' perceptions that the chatbot is attempting to manipulate them.
Methodologically, this study demonstrates a prompt-based approach to manipulating AI chatbot anthropomorphism.

Rather than relying exclusively on fixed names, avatars, or scripted language, the chatbot was instructed to communicate in a more humanlike manner while adapting its responses to each conversational turn.
The manipulation was effective.
This approach preserves the responsiveness of LLM-enabled interactions and may be extended to experimental manipulations of other perceived characteristics, such as warmth, empathy, or humor.
Nevertheless, researchers should continue to assess possible effects on response coherence, perceived intelligence, and other chatbot evaluations.
This study has several limitations.
First, participants were recruited through Prolific and were limited to U.S. adults who reported current e-cigarette use.
The sample was younger, more highly educated, and included a greater proportion of White participants than the general U.S. population (U. S. Census Bureau, 2024a Bureau, , 2024b)).

text.text: Generalization to the broader population, adolescents, or other groups of people who vape should therefore be approached cautiously.
Second, the study did not measure dispositional anthropomorphism because of questionnaire-length constraints.

Random assignment should have minimized systematic differences between conditions, but individuals may differ in their general tendency to attribute human qualities to nonhuman agents (Waytz et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Random assignment should have minimized systematic differences between conditions, but individuals may differ in their general tendency to attribute human qualities to nonhuman agents <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">(Waytz et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Future research should examine whether this tendency moderates the effects of chatbot design on mindful and mindless anthropomorphism, trust, and reactance.
The study also did not measure perceived threat to freedom, a central antecedent of reactance (Dillard & Shen, 2005; Rains, 2013).
text.formatted: The study also did not measure perceived threat to freedom, a central antecedent of reactance <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Dillard & Shen, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Rains, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Including this construct would permit a more complete test of whether anthropomorphic design reduces reactance by making the message appear less freedom threatening.
Third, participants interacted with the chatbot for only three conversational rounds.
The limited exposure may have prevented the effects of anthropomorphism from fully developing.
Additionally, the study captured users' responses immediately after the interaction and therefore could not assess whether the observed effects persisted over time.

Further research should employ longer interactions and longitudinal designs to examine how users' responses to anthropomorphic chatbots evolve with repeated exposure and whether reductions in reactance are long-lasting beyond the immediate interaction.
Finally, the study examined one health topic using the GPT-4.1-mini API.
Replication across vaccination, medication adherence, cancer screening, and other health contexts is necessary to establish generalizability.
Comparisons across LLMs are also important because models may differ in their conversational styles, capabilities, and adherence to experimental prompts.
Cross-model sensitivity analyses would help determine whether the observed patterns reflect general processes of chatbot anthropomorphism or characteristics of the particular model used.

This study demonstrates that interacting with an anthropomorphic AI chatbot reduced psychological reactance compared with reading a static health message, although this advantage did not extend to attitudes toward vaping or intentions to quit following a brief interaction.

More importantly, the findings reveal distinct pathways linking anthropomorphism to psychological reactance: mindful anthropomorphism was indirectly associated with lower reactance through greater trust in the chatbot, whereas mindless anthropomorphism was directly associated with lower reactance.
Neither dimension was significantly associated with perceived persuasive intent, although greater perceived persuasive intent was associated with higher reactance.

By distinguishing these pathways, this study extends anthropomorphism and CASA/MASA research and advances our understanding of how humanlike characteristics shape responses to AImediated health persuasion.
Overall, these findings support the potential effectiveness of anthropomorphic AI chatbots as a communication approach for vaping cessation and, more broadly, for health communication.
